read.sections.0.heading.source: Where an AI answer is made

read.sections.0.text.source: When you ask an AI tool a question, your device usually doesn't make the answer itself. Some small tools can run on a phone or laptop. But most of the time, the question travels to a data centre, a large building full of computers. Its chips do huge numbers of sums each second. They use a lot of electricity and get very hot, so many data centres use water to cool them. The International Energy Agency estimated that in 2024, all the world's data centres used about 1.5% of its electricity. It thinks about 15% of that was for AI. The rest was for other work. Data centres also run websites, videos and messages. The agency expects data centres to use about twice as much by 2030, mostly because of AI. That is a forecast, not a measurement, and the agency says it is uncertain.
read.sections.0.text.back: When you ask an AI tool a question, your device usually does not make the answer itself. Some small tools can run on a phone or laptop, but mostly the question travels to a data centre, a huge building full of computers. The chips inside calculate huge amounts of numbers every second. These chips use a lot of electricity and get very hot, so many data centres use water to help cool them. The International Energy Agency estimates that in 2024 all the data centres in the world used about 1.5 percent of the world's electricity, and thinks about 15 percent of that went to AI. The rest went to other work, because data centres also run websites, videos and messages. The agency expects data centres to use roughly twice as much electricity by 2030, mostly because of AI. This number is a forecast, not a measurement, and the agency says it is uncertain.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Usually, an AI answer is not made in your device. Some small tools do work on a phone. But most questions go to a data centre. This is a big building full of computers. Its chips do huge amounts of maths. They use a lot of power and get very hot. Water often helps to cool them. In 2024, all data centres used about 1.5% of the world's power. Only a small part was for AI. Data centres also run videos and messages. Experts think the power they use may double by 2030, mostly because of AI. That is a forecast. It is a guess, not a fact yet.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Usually an AI answer is not made in your device. Some small tools can run on a phone, but most questions go to a data centre. A data centre is a big building full of computers. The chips inside can do huge amounts of sums. They use a lot of electricity and get very hot. Water often helps cool them. In 2024 all data centres used about 1.5 percent of the world's electricity. Only a small part went to AI. Data centres also run videos and messages. Experts think that by 2030 the electricity used may double. AI is the main cause. That is a forecast. It is a guess, not yet a fact.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Chips need minerals and a few factories
read.sections.1.heading.back: Chips need minerals and only a few factories

read.sections.1.text.source: Chips are made from materials dug out of the ground. Some need rare minerals, which are often mined in ways that harm nature. Very few factories can make the most powerful chips. A 2021 chip industry study found that 92% of the most advanced chips were made in Taiwan. So a problem in one place could slow chip supplies around the world. Old chips and computers also become electronic waste, which can contain harmful metals such as mercury and lead.
read.sections.1.text.back: Chips are made from materials dug up from the ground. Some kinds of chips need rare minerals, which are often mined in ways that damage nature. Only a few factories can make the most powerful chips. A 2021 chip-industry study found that 92 percent of the most advanced chips were made in Taiwan, so a problem in one place can slow chip deliveries around the world. Old chips and computers also become electronic waste, which may contain dangerous metals such as mercury and lead.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Singapore, Johor and Batam make choices
read.sections.2.heading.back: Singapore, Johor and Batam choose a path

read.sections.2.text.source: Data centres need land, power and water. So where they go is a choice for governments. By the early 2020s, data centres used about 7% of Singapore's electricity. Singapore paused new ones in 2019. From 2022, it let in only a few that met strict rules on saving energy. Many companies built across the border in Johor, in Malaysia, and on Batam, in Indonesia. In the first ten months of 2024, Malaysia drew more than 31 billion US dollars of investment in data centres. The energy agency expects data centres to cause as much as a fifth of the growth in Malaysia's power use by 2030. Building them brings work that ends when the building is finished. Running them brings some long-term jobs. These often need special training. Some experts say data centres bring far fewer jobs than they promise. People nearby worry about water and power cuts. In November 2025, Johor stopped saying yes to the most basic kinds of data centres. These can use far more water. The rules are still changing.
read.sections.2.text.back: Data centres need land, electricity and water, so choosing where to build them is something governments must decide. By the early 2020s data centres used about 7 percent of all the electricity in Singapore. Singapore paused new data centres in 2019, and since 2022 has allowed only a few that pass strict energy-saving rules. So many companies went to build across the border in Johor in Malaysia, and on Batam island in Indonesia. In the first ten months of 2024 Malaysia received more than 31 billion US dollars of investment in data centres. The energy agency expects that by 2030 data centres could cause up to one fifth of the growth in electricity use in Malaysia. Construction brings jobs, but those jobs end when the building is finished. Looking after a data centre gives some long-term jobs, which often need specialised training. Some experts say data centres create far fewer jobs than promised. People who live nearby worry about water and power cuts. In November 2025 Johor stopped approving the most basic data centres, which can use much more water than other kinds. These rules are still changing.
read.sections.2.text.note: Batam is written บาตัม (and Johor ยะโฮร์), the usual Thai names, as the brief asks for real places. The checker warns that the Latin “Batam” is missing; that is expected. Neither is in KEY_TERMS: please confirm the spellings. “31 billion” is written 31 พันล้าน so the digits stay as in the English.

watch.summary.source: This animated lesson explains why AI data centres use so much power. The video says that since 2019, more than a thousand huge AI data centres have been built. It says each one can use as much water as a small town, and as much power as a small city. Inside are thousands of computers with special chips. The chips do trillions of sums each second. All this work makes them very hot. Engineers cool them with water or special liquids. They also send data with light, which wastes less power. But AI tools keep getting bigger, so they need more and more power. The video asks if we could build smaller tools for smaller jobs. It ends with a question: how much of the planet should we use for smarter machines?
watch.summary.back: This animated lesson explains why AI data centres use so much electricity. The video says that since 2019 more than a thousand large AI data centres have been built, and says each may use as much water as a small town and as much electricity as a small city. Inside are thousands of computers with special chips. These chips can do trillions of sums every second. All this work makes them very hot. Engineers cool them with water or special liquids, and also send data with light, which wastes less electricity. But AI tools keep getting bigger, so they need more and more electricity. The video asks whether we could build smaller tools for smaller jobs, and ends with the question: how much of our planet should we use for smarter machines?

educatorNotes.0.source: The numbers are dated and scoped. Electricity: the International Energy Agency's Energy and AI report (April 2025) estimated that all data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, about 1.5% of the world's electricity; AI servers were about 15% of data-centre electricity (24% of server electricity) that year. It projects about 945 TWh by 2030, slightly more than Japan uses now, with AI the main driver and with stated uncertainty (the pace of AI use, efficiency gains, bottlenecks). These figures were read in Scientific American (10 April 2025) and AFP via The Star (10 April 2025); the IEA's own pages refused access on 8 November 2026, so check them if you can. At the launch, the IEA's head said data centres were on course to account for “as much as one-fifth” of Malaysia's electricity-demand growth to 2030 (a projection, not a measurement; reported by Hydrocarbon Engineering and GreenTechLead). On the device: some small models run on phones and laptops (for example Apple's roughly 3-billion-parameter model, 2024), while most large tools run in data centres. Taiwan's 92% of the most advanced chip-making is from a 2021 Semiconductor Industry Association study (Reuters, 1 April 2021). Minerals and e-waste (mercury, lead) are from UNEP (21 September 2024). UNEP's “800 kg of materials for a 2 kg computer” (no source given) stays out.
educatorNotes.0.back: These figures carry dates and scope. Electricity: the International Energy Agency's Energy and AI report (IEA, April 2025) estimates that all data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, about 1.5 percent of the world's electricity. In that year AI servers used about 15 percent of data-centre electricity (24 percent of server electricity). The report expects this to rise to about 945 TWh by 2030, slightly more than Japan uses today, with AI the main driver, and notes uncertainties (speed of AI adoption, efficiency gains and bottlenecks). These figures were read from Scientific American (10 April 2025) and AFP via The Star (10 April 2025), because the IEA's own page was not accessible on 8 November 2026; check that page if possible. At the launch, the IEA head said data centres are likely to cause “up to one fifth” of the growth in electricity demand in Malaysia to 2030 (a projection, not a measurement; reported by Hydrocarbon Engineering and GreenTechLead). On-device: some small models run on phones and laptops (such as Apple's roughly 3-billion-parameter model, 2024); most large tools run in data centres. The 92 percent figure for the most advanced chip manufacturing in Taiwan comes from a 2021 Semiconductor Industry Association study (Reuters, 1 April 2021). Minerals and e-waste (mercury, lead) come from UNEP (21 September 2024); UNEP's figure of “800 kg of materials to make a 2 kg computer” (no source given) was not used.

educatorNotes.1.source: Singapore, Johor and Batam: Singapore paused new data centres in 2019; reports put their share of its electricity at about 7% (AP dates it to 2019, Kontinentalist to 2021, DatacenterDynamics in 2022 says over 7%). From 2022 a pilot call admitted a few new ones that met strict efficiency rules (a PUE below 1.3, top green-building certification); about 80 MW went to four operators, and a 2024 Green Data Centre Roadmap promised at least 300 MW more. Johor grew from nearly nothing in 2019 to at least 1.6 GW planned (AP, February 2025), and Malaysia drew over US$31 billion of data-centre investment in the first 10 months of 2024 (Knight Frank, via AP). Jobs: building work ends when the building is finished; a typical data centre has 30 to 50 permanent jobs and large ones up to 200, according to Good Jobs First, a US group (via AP and an ISEAS commentary, March 2025). That figure is not measured for Johor, so it is not in the learner text. In November 2025 Johor stopped approving Tier 1 and Tier 2 data centres, which can use up to 200 times more water than higher tiers; in February 2026 Malaysia's prime minister said approvals for new non-AI data centres had been limited. Rules change quickly: check the latest before teaching the third section. Data centres also run websites, videos and messages, not only AI. The claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW06.md.
